paras: The lynching of Thomas Collins was the hanging by a mob of a Black man at Bunkie, Louisiana, first reported on August 1, 1915. Collins was accused of shooting and wounding a policeman who had tried to arrest him. A special grand jury called to investigate the lynching reported that it could not find enough evidence to hold anyone responsible.

According to a wire brief printed on August 1, a Black man at Bunkie had wounded with a shot a policeman who wanted to arrest him, and was then lynched by a mob. A later brief named him as Thomas Collins, described him as "accused of wounding a policeman," and said he "was hanged by a mob." The coverage gives no date for the lynching, no size for the mob, and no account of whether Collins was taken from jail or seized elsewhere.

Judge Lafargue called a special session of the grand jury to investigate "the recent lynching of a negro in Bunkie County." The grand jury completed its inquiry and reported to the court that it had "failed to secure sufficient evidence to hold any person responsible for the lynching." No report of arrests, indictments or a trial was found.

The lynching reached the press only as one-sentence items in news-in-brief columns. The earliest found was in a Milwaukee German-language weekly, Der Sonntagsbote und der Seebote, whose August 1 roundup of wire news set the lynching between a street-car crash in Pennsylvania and a fire in Alaska, stating the shooting of the policeman as fact. The Honolulu Star-Bulletin carried the only version found that named the victim, on August 10, and it framed the shooting as an accusation.

In Louisiana, the grand jury's finding ran as an identical state-news paragraph in the Caldwell Watchman of Columbia on August 6, the Madison Journal of Tallulah on August 7, and the Rice Belt Journal of Welsh on August 13. These items did not name the victim, calling him only "a negro," and reported the result without comment. No coverage of the lynching was found in the Black press.

A mob hanged or lynched the man (A1, A4) for allegedly wounding a policeman (A1, A4), and a grand jury investigated it as a lynching (A2); the size of the mob is not given, but the papers call it a mob.
A wire brief (A1), a separate news brief (A4) and a Louisiana state-news item on the grand jury (A2) agree that a Black man was lynched at Bunkie; only A4 gives the name Thomas Collins.

accounts.label: Wire briefs
accounts.gist: A Black man at Bunkie, La., who had shot and wounded a policeman trying to arrest him (A1), named as Thomas Collins and 'accused of wounding a policeman' (A4), was lynched or hanged by a mob.

accounts.label: Grand jury report
accounts.gist: A special grand jury called by Judge Lafargue investigated the recent lynching of a negro in 'Bunkie County' and found insufficient evidence to hold anyone responsible.

framing.detail: One-sentence items in news-in-brief columns: a German-language weekly's 'Drahtfunk aus aller Welt' roundup (A1) and a Honolulu paper (A4); A1 states the shooting as fact while A4 says 'accused of wounding a policeman.'
Louisiana weeklies ran the grand jury result as a state-news paragraph without comment, the victim unnamed as 'a negro.'
